title: Design a job scheduler
dek: "Ask for a rating an hour after delivery." "Pay every restaurant at 9 pm." "Sync menus every 15 minutes." Zotato has crores of jobs that must run at a set time. Run each one close to on time, never lose one, and survive the moment 9 pm arrives.

items: Store every job with the time it should run. Group jobs by the minute they're due, so finding what to run now never means scanning the whole table.
A scheduler claims each due job with a lease ("mine for 30 seconds") and puts it on a queue. If the worker dies, the lease runs out and another picks the job up.
That means a job can occasionally run twice. Make every job safe to repeat, using the job's id, rather than chase "exactly once".
A recurring job is one job at a time: when it finishes, add its next run.
9 pm brings lakhs of jobs due in the same second. A queue spreads the burst, and jobs that don't need the exact second get a little random delay.
Schedule a job to run once at a time (a rating reminder at 21:42) or on a repeat (every day at 21:00, every 15 minutes).
Run it within a few seconds of its time; retry if it fails; never silently lose it.
Cancel or change a job before it runs; see what ran, when, and with what result.
Out of scope here: the work the jobs do (sending, paying), and chains of jobs that depend on each other.

body.label: Qualities to aim for
head: Quality
Target
rows: Started within 5 seconds of its time, even at 9 pm
A job that was accepted runs, or is marked failed after its retries
A job that runs twice does its work once
About 1.2 crore jobs a day, lakhs of them due at 21:00

items: Rating reminders: 1 crore orders a day, one reminder each. Add payouts, syncs and the rest: about 1.2 crore jobs a day, around 140 a second on average.
Evenings are busier: reminders follow dinner deliveries, so 9 to 11 pm runs at around 500 a second.
The spike: 3 lakh restaurants' 9 pm payouts are all due at 21:00:00. Start them in 5 seconds and that's 60,000 a second for those 5 seconds, far above normal.
Storage: 1.2 crore rows a day at about 500 bytes is 6 GB a day. Keep finished jobs for a few weeks, then archive them.

Job: `id`, `kind`, `payload`, `run_at` (stored in UTC), `minute` (the minute it's due, for grouping), `repeat` (none, or a schedule like "every day 21:00 IST"), `status` (waiting, claimed, done, failed, cancelled), `lease_until`, `attempts`.
Run: `job_id`, `started_at`, `finished_at`, `result`, `worker`. One row per attempt, for seeing what happened.

body.label: API
body.x:
POST   /jobs        { "id": "rate_91", "kind": "rating_reminder", "run_at": "2026-11-06T21:42+05:30", "payload": { "order": "#91" } }  → 201
POST   /jobs        { "id": "payouts", "kind": "daily_payouts", "repeat": "every day 21:00 Asia/Kolkata" }  → 201
DELETE /jobs/rate_91  → 204
GET    /jobs/payouts/runs?last=7  → 200 { "runs": [ … ] }
body.say: Add a one-off or repeating job, with your own id so adding it twice changes nothing. Cancel one. See its last runs.

body.cap: Services add jobs with a run time. Schedulers look only at minutes that are due, claim each job with a lease and put it on a queue. Executors run it and record the result: done, retry later, or the next run of a repeating job.

body.x: Schedulers only decide what's due and hand it over; executors do the work. A slow job (a payout that calls a bank) can't stop the scheduler from starting the next minute's jobs on time.

body.name: First try
body.what: Every second, query "status = waiting and run_at <= now" across all jobs.
body.use: Works for a few thousand jobs.
body.avoid: With crores of rows, every scan reads a lot, and two scheduler machines happily pick the same job.
body.ex: At 21:00:00 both schedulers read the same 3 lakh payout jobs; restaurants get paid twice.
body.like: Reading the whole diary every second to see if anything is due.

body.name: Better
body.kind: GROUPED BY MINUTE, CLAIMED WITH A LEASE
body.what: Index jobs by the minute they're due. Each second, a scheduler looks at every minute up to now and claims a batch in one update: status claimed, lease_until now + 30 s, only if the job is waiting or its lease has run out. Split each minute's jobs across schedulers by a hash of the job id, or just let them all claim with SKIP LOCKED.
body.use: Each look is small, and a job can only be claimed by one scheduler at a time.
body.avoid: Claims must be atomic (an update with a condition, or SKIP LOCKED in SQL). A lease too short expires while the job is still running.
body.ex: At 21:00:00, three schedulers each claim their third of the payout jobs and queue them in a few seconds.
body.like: A diary with a page per minute: at 9 pm you open only the 9 pm page.

body.cap: Worker A claims the 21:00 payout with a 30-second lease and dies 10 seconds in, before its next heartbeat. When the lease ends, worker B claims it and runs it. If A was only paused, the job's id makes its late work harmless.

items: While a job runs, the executor extends its lease every few seconds. If it stops (crash, pause, lost network), the lease runs out and the job is claimed again.
The executor resets the lease when it takes the job off the queue; the scheduler's lease only needs to cover the wait in the queue.

So a job may start twice: once by a worker that only looked dead. Each claim gets a new number, and writes carrying an old number are refused (fencing). Give every job's work an id ("payout restaurant 214 for 6 Nov"), and let whatever it writes to skip a repeat of that id.
Count attempts. After a few failures, mark the job failed and alert someone, instead of retrying for ever.
Retries wait longer each time, with a bit of randomness, so a failing bank isn't hit by every retry at once.
Jobs due in the same second all land on the queue together; executors work through them as fast as they can. The queue is what absorbs the spike.
Jobs that only need "around" a time (menu syncs, reports) get a random delay of a few minutes when they're created, so they don't all line up on the hour.
Priorities: payouts and reminders shouldn't wait behind a big report. Use separate queues, as in the notifications question.
A repeating job has one waiting row at a time. When a run finishes (or is claimed, for jobs that must keep their rhythm), add the next one in the same transaction.
After an outage, some jobs are late. Decide per kind: payouts run once now; a 15-minute sync skips the runs it missed and does the next.
Store times in UTC and keep the job's time zone with it, so "21:00 IST" stays 21:00 in India even if a server's clock is set to UTC.
Junior / mid: a jobs table with run times, a worker that runs due jobs, retries, a queue.
Senior: grouping by minute, atomic claims with leases, repeat-safe jobs, the 9 pm numbers, recurring jobs.
Lead: splitting the work across schedulers, missed runs after downtime, priorities, fencing a paused worker, retries with backoff and jitter.
"Run a job at an exact millisecond?" Not needed here; say what accuracy you promise (seconds) and why.
"Lakhs of jobs for one restaurant's offers?" Store one job that expands into many small ones when it runs, instead of lakhs of rows up front.
"Cancel a job that's already running?" Mark it cancelled; the executor checks between steps and stops cleanly.
"Why not cron on one machine?" One machine is one failure away from missing the 9 pm payouts, and can't spread lakhs of jobs.
"How do you test it?" Kill executors mid-job and pause schedulers, then check every job ran, none did its work twice, and the 9 pm jobs started within 5 seconds.

body.x: 9 pm is a spike at a known time, like a flash sale. The flash-sale challenge is practice for surviving one.
